claims.text: The as-synthesized multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles have a nominally homogeneous elemental distribution.
Rapid cooling freezes in a chemically homogeneous, ordered atomic configuration.
Rapidly cooled nanoparticles retain structural and chemical integrity at high temperature better than slowly cooled nanoparticles.
Changing the synthesis cooling rate or post-synthesis thermal treatment modulates initial atomic ordering and chemical segregation.
Initial atomic ordering or chemical homogenization mediates the rate of diffusion-driven phase segregation and precipitation.
Atomic ordering can lead multicomponent alloys into different crystalline, intermetallic, or disordered microstructural states.
The reduced atomic mobility produced by rapid cooling persists sufficiently to suppress deleterious diffusion during subsequent high-temperature service.
Suppressing diffusion limits phase segregation and precipitate formation at high temperature.
Slow cooling permits partial atomic segregation during synthesis.
Partial segregation generated during slow cooling makes nanoparticles more susceptible to thermally driven transformations.
Rapidly cooled nanoparticles will show less phase segregation and precipitate formation than normally cooled nanoparticles after high-temperature exposure.
Rapidly cooled nanoparticles will maintain greater structural homogeneity than normally cooled nanoparticles after high-temperature exposure.
Composition and annealing temperature can govern phase stability and the length scale of phase decomposition in multicomponent alloys.
Particle size, surface energy, and synthesis-method differences may alter the relationship between cooling rate and stability.
Microstructural stability is associated with preservation of catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
